Subject: One form, three reminders, set once
Preview text: Build the testimonial ask in Senja instead of messaging each quiet student yourself.

Hi there,

Senja collects text and video testimonials, and the part worth your attention is the asking: you build one collection form, switch follow-ups on, then send it to your current or most recent cohort.

Senja reckons a simple or multistep form takes about 60 seconds to build. From then on the chasing is bounded — up to three reminder emails, at 1, 3 and 7 days after the invite, and only to students who haven't answered.

Video is one option, not the price of entry. Your student opens a personalised page and leaves a text or video answer, with no account to create and nothing to install. Senja puts that at about 30 seconds.

Reminders only go out on invites you send after switching them on, so the form comes first. A free account is where it gets built: the questions, the page your cohort will open, the follow-up schedule, all before anything is sent.

The free plan holds 15 text and video testimonials, and new ones past that stay hidden until you upgrade.

Get started for free → https://app.senja.io/signup

- the Senja team

emails.single_idea: Asking your cohort for testimonials is a setup job, not a correspondence job — you build the form once and switch the chasing on once, instead of deciding all over again whether to message each quiet student.
emails.selection_reason: This reader's documented problem is not 'I need a testimonial widget', it is 'I don't know how to get testimonials and I don't want to keep nagging people' (P1), plus 'praise doesn't become a testimonial unless you ask, and asking late makes it weaker' (P3). The one thing Senja's evidence can honestly change about that is the shape of the work: the ask becomes a form you build once (E150) and a capped reminder schedule you switch on once (E27), and the student's side is a page they can answer without an account (R3). Every number here is checkable before they spend anything, which suits a self-serve free signup.
emails.next_step_decision: Whether to run the next cohort's testimonial ask through one form plus capped reminders, instead of writing the messages themselves.
emails.next_step_value: A free account is where the form actually gets built — they can create the collection form, see the questions and the student-facing page their cohort will open, and turn the follow-up schedule on before sending anything.
emails.next_step_limit: Signing up shows them the form and the reminder settings; it does not tell them how their students will react, how many will answer, or what the finished testimonials will look like on their sales page. Triggering requests automatically from a course platform is a paid feature and is not part of this step. The free plan holds 15 testimonials.

reader_verdicts.what_it_sells: A testimonial collection tool — I build one form, it sends my cohort a personalised page where they leave text or video, and it chases the non-responders three times so I don't have to DM anyone.
reader_verdicts.relevance_feedback: Profile-supported: I run cohorts and I do need testimonials, and the email's premise — that the hard part is the asking, not the displaying — lands on something real for me. Email-only: that I'm currently 'messaging each quiet student yourself' (preview text). That's an assumption about my process; the profile doesn't establish how I ask today, or that I use any tool. Also email-only: that I need video specifically. The 'Video is one option, not the price of entry' line is reassuring but it's answering a worry they assigned me. Unknown: whether I already have something that does this, and whether my cohort is at the right point in its lifecycle for a 'current or most recent cohort' send. Nothing here contradicts my situation.
assumed_experiences: That I currently chase students individually by message (email-only, from preview text)
That I have a current or most recent cohort available to invite right now (email-only; plausible for a cohort operator but not established)
That video testimonials feel like a barrier I'm worried about (email-only)
That I have no testimonial collection tool in place (email-only; relationship and tooling unspecified in profile)
reader_verdicts.problem_now: Documented importance, uncertain urgency. Getting testimonials out of a cohort matters to me and the timing-of-the-ask problem is real — ask late and you get vague praise. But nothing in my profile sets a deadline, and the email doesn't claim one either, which I appreciate. It's a 'should have done this last cohort' problem rather than a fire.
reader_verdicts.stopped_at: Reminders only go out on invites you send after switching them on, so the form comes first.
reader_verdicts.biggest_doubt: The free plan cap. 15 text and video testimonials combined is roughly one cohort's worth, and the email says new ones past that 'stay hidden until you upgrade' — so the thing I'd use it for every cohort has a price I don't know. I'd rather see the number before I build forms and send invites to real students and then find out the ask is paywalled.
reader_verdicts.to_click_it_would_have_to: I would have clicked if this email had told me what the paid plan costs per month, since 15 testimonials is less than one cohort and the whole point is doing this every cohort.

Not onboarding, not a nurture note to an existing user: this reader has never used Senja. The current dossier narrows the usable slice to cohort-based course operators, so the email is written to someone who sells the next cohort from a page, and the documented next action is the self-serve free signup on the offer sheet (https://app.senja.io/signup). I did not adopt the segment's 'needs student results on camera before the next cohort launch' framing as a fact about the recipient: the research explicitly says the imminent-launch-deadline situation is not established, so the email assumes a cohort that is running or has just finished and never asserts a deadline. brief.reader_segment: A course creator or coach who needs student results on camera before the next cohort launch
brief.promise: Asking your students for a testimonial can be a thing you set up once, rather than a string of messages you have to keep deciding whether to send.
brief.orientation: For a small course or coaching team collecting student feedback for course and cohort sales pages, Senja is a tool for requesting text or video testimonials and displaying or reusing the responses.
brief.arc: Single email, so the arc is inside it: open on the part of the job the reader actually dreads (the asking and the chasing, not the deciding), turn on the reframe that this is a setup task with a cap on it, show the three mechanics that make that true — the form you build once, the three reminders at days 1, 3 and 7 that only go to students who stayed quiet, and the 30-second answer page with no account to create — then ask for the free account while the cohort is still fresh.
brief.sequence_rationale: One email was requested in so many words, so everything the reader needs to decide has to be in it: the mechanism, the student-side burden, and the free entry terms. I led with the asking/chasing argument rather than the display argument (the alternative) for three reasons. First, it is where the verified problems are strongest: P1 and P3 are both about the ask, and the previous campaign's rework note landed on exactly this framing — asking is a setup job, not a correspondence job. Second, the display argument assumes the reader already has testimonials in hand; the research shows a creator who does not know how to get them, so display answers a question they have not reached. Third, the asking argument is carried by evidence with numbers a stranger can check (60 seconds, three reminders at 1/3/7, about 30 seconds, no account) rather than by capability adjectives. The objection I assigned is the student-burden one, because R3 answers it directly. I deliberately did not assign the 'will my students think I'm pushy' objection: the dossier states explicitly that student reception is not established, so the writer would have no honest answer and would invent one.

emails.selection_reason: This reader's documented problem is not 'I need a testimonial widget', it is 'I don't know how to get testimonials and I don't want to keep nagging people' (P1), plus 'praise doesn't become a testimonial unless you ask, and asking late makes it weaker' (P3). The one thing Senja's evidence can honestly change about that is the shape of the work: the ask becomes a form you build once (E150) and a capped reminder schedule you switch on once (E27), and the student's side is a page they can answer without an account (R3). Every number here is checkable before they spend anything, which suits a self-serve free signup.
emails.job: Get a cohort course operator to create a free Senja account and build the collection form they will send to their current or most recent cohort.
emails.single_idea: Asking your cohort for testimonials is a setup job, not a correspondence job — you build the form once and switch the chasing on once, instead of deciding all over again whether to message each quiet student.
emails.felt_need: A newly launched course creator reports not knowing how to obtain testimonials and feeling reluctant to ask for reviews because it could seem pushy. Neera reports that praise does not automatically become strong testimonials: asking appropriately and promptly matters, and delayed requests can produce weaker recollections.
emails.mechanism: You build one collection form — Senja says a simple or multistep one takes about 60 seconds — send it to your students, and turn follow-ups on. From then on the chasing is bounded and automatic: up to three reminder emails, at 1, 3 and 7 days after the original invite, and only to students who haven't responded. Your student opens a personalised page and leaves a text or video answer; Senja describes it as about 30 seconds, with no account to create and nothing to install. Setting it up requires a Senja account, which is where the free plan comes in.

alternative_arguments.selection_reason: The same reader's second documented uncertainty is 'where should I collect and display them?' (P2). This is a different commercial bet: not 'here is a calmer way to ask' but 'the answer you collect is a page asset and a reel, and putting it on your cohort page doesn't involve code'. It leads with E99 and E24 — both LEAD-ranked — and reuses none of the primary's proof, so a cold reader is genuinely choosing between two reasons to act rather than two phrasings of one.
alternative_arguments.single_idea: A student's video answer is not a file you then have to do something with — it goes straight onto your cohort page, into your emails and into clips, without touching code.
alternative_arguments.felt_need: The same creator is unsure whether incentives would seem fake, whether to request video or written testimonials, and where to collect and display them.
alternative_arguments.mechanism: Once a testimonial is in Senja it is already a publishable object: you can add it to your site without coding, use collected videos in widgets, emails and remixed clips, and build a Wall of Love from your reviews in a few clicks — the same answer, in several places, without a rebuild each time.
alternative_arguments.belief_shift: Before: publishing a student testimonial on the cohort page is a small web job I have to schedule or outsource. After: the collecting and the publishing are the same tool, and the website part is a no-code step.
must_not_say: No conversion, enrollment or revenue claim — E99's source says 'increase your conversion rates' and that part is out of scope; only the no-code embedding is checkable.
Don't claim a Wall of Love or widget makes testimonials look more trustworthy or professional; display options are documented, perceived trustworthiness is not.
Don't recommend video over text (or the reverse) as better for selling a cohort — the research shows the reader asking this and the evidence does not answer it.
Don't name widget styles as a catalogue; one named format is orientation, twenty is a feature list.
Don't imply the reader already has testimonials collected — write it conditionally ('once a student has answered').
Don't mention the case study generator, Chrome extension, Slack bot, MCP, Zapier/API, rich snippets or translation; none of them is this argument.
The product supplies format, collection and display options, but cannot establish which format is best or whether rewards will seem fake; one question cannot receive both text and video.
alternative_arguments.objection: Embedding things on my course or sales page is the bit I usually have to pay someone for.
alternative_arguments.next_step_decision: Whether Senja is where their student testimonials should live, given that the page they sell the cohort from has to show them.
alternative_arguments.next_step_value: A free account lets them see the actual display side: adding a testimonial to a website without coding, and turning collected reviews into a Wall of Love in a few clicks.
alternative_arguments.next_step_limit: It does not show how the embed will look inside their specific course platform's template, and it does not establish any effect on enrollment. The free plan holds 15 testimonials; beyond that, new ones are hidden until you upgrade.
alternative_arguments.subject_strategy: Lead on the gap between having a good student quote and it being on the page — the reader recognises that gap instantly. Avoid 'social proof' and avoid naming widget formats in the subject.

emails.belief_shift: Before: getting testimonials means personally chasing students one message at a time, and I'll have to keep deciding how hard to push. After: it's one form and one switch — the reminders are capped at three, on a fixed schedule, and only reach the students who haven't answered.
must_not_say: Do not promise that students won't find the ask pushy, or that they will respond, participate or reply warmly — the dossier states reception and participation are not established by this evidence.
Do not claim that asking this way produces stronger, more concrete or more 'transformational' testimonials, or better recollection. P3 is the reader's observation, not a Senja result.

Do not merge the two durations into one speed claim: 60 seconds is Senja's figure for building the form, about 30 seconds is Senja's description of the student's answer. Neither describes how long the whole collection takes, and '30 seconds' is Senja's description, not a measured average of real students.
Do not imply reminders reach students who were invited before follow-ups were switched on — they don't.

Do not present auto-triggered requests from a course platform (Kajabi, Teachable, Thinkific, Stripe and so on) as part of this; auto-collect needs a Starter or Pro plan and this reader's platform is unknown.
Do not imply unlimited collection on the free plan. Free is 15 video and text testimonials, and new ones past that are hidden until you upgrade — say it plainly if the free plan is mentioned.
Do not raise incentives, rewards or e-gifts: the reader's own worry is whether an incentive 'seems fake', and the evidence cannot answer that.

Keep the display suite off the page entirely — widgets, Wall of Love, case study generator, reels, Chrome extension, Slack bot, MCP, Zapier/API, rich snippets, translation, seats and projects. This reader is deciding how to ask, not buying a proof platform.
No enrollment, conversion or revenue claim, and no claim about filling the next cohort.
Do not assert the reader has a launch deadline, a half-empty cohort, a past failed attempt at collecting testimonials, or a particular course platform.
Do not use the 20,000-user figure as evidence that this works for course creators; it isn't assigned here and it argues nothing this email needs.
Forms and invitations provide a way to ask, but reduced reluctance, non-pushy reception and successful participation are not established by the selected evidence.
Event-triggered requests require a connected platform; current audience stack compatibility and stronger, more concrete recollections are not established by the selected evidence.
emails.objection: My students are busy and half of them won't want to film themselves — am I about to put a chore in front of people who just finished paying me?
emails.tone: Matter-of-fact and slightly brisk. Short, one-breath sentences in the narrative part, tighter and more mechanical where the numbers land. Dry rather than hyped; no exclamation marks, no 'imagine if'.
emails.next_step_decision: Whether to run the next cohort's testimonial ask through one form plus capped reminders, instead of writing the messages themselves.
emails.next_step_value: A free account is where the form actually gets built — they can create the collection form, see the questions and the student-facing page their cohort will open, and turn the follow-up schedule on before sending anything.
emails.next_step_limit: Signing up shows them the form and the reminder settings; it does not tell them how their students will react, how many will answer, or what the finished testimonials will look like on their sales page. Triggering requests automatically from a course platform is a paid feature and is not part of this step. The free plan holds 15 testimonials.
emails.subject_strategy: This reader already believes testimonials work, so a subject about why proof sells is dead. Earn the open on the part they're avoiding: the chasing. Something that signals a limit or a mechanic — the asking being finite, or done once — rather than a benefit. Avoid 'social proof', avoid 'grow your cohort', avoid question-mark curiosity bait.

brief.voice_notes: The reader is a creator, not a software buyer: 'students' and 'cohort', not 'customers', 'users' or 'leads'. Senja's house register — direct, dry, a joke next to a concrete number — fits, but the joke is never at a student's expense. Say 'testimonials'; use 'social proof' at most once and never in the first line. Senja's own figures should read as Senja's figures where they are soft ('Senja reckons about 30 seconds'), and flatly where they are structural (three reminders, days 1, 3 and 7).
